lessons.title: Software RAID with mdadm
lessons.goal:
Build a RAID 1 (mirror) from two disks, watch it survive the failure of one, and rebuild it.

Why it matters: RAID protects against disk failure (not against deletion or corruption: it is not a backup). Knowing the commands is essential when a disk dies at 3 a.m.

setup.note: These steps use sudo and loop devices (image files acting as disks). They create a volume group called `labvg` and remove it at the end. They never touch real disks.

steps.title: RAID levels in short
steps.text:
- **RAID 0**: striping, speed, no protection.
- **RAID 1**: mirror, survives one disk loss, half the capacity.
- **RAID 5**: striping with one parity, survives one disk, needs 3+.
- **RAID 6**: two parities, survives two disks.
- **RAID 10**: striped mirrors: speed and protection.

Linux software RAID is the `md` driver, managed by `mdadm`. We use two 100 MB loop devices.

run.cmd: truncate -s 100M r1.img r2.img; L1=$(sudo losetup -f --show r1.img); L2=$(sudo losetup -f --show r2.img); echo $L1 $L2

steps.title: Create a mirror
steps.text: `--level=1 --raid-devices=2` builds a RAID 1 from the two devices. The new device appears as `/dev/md/labmd` (a link to `/dev/mdN`).

run.output:
md127 : active raid1 loopN[1] loopN[0]
      101376 blocks super 1.2 [2/2] [UU]

steps.title: Inspect the array
steps.text: `mdadm --detail` shows the state, number of devices and each member.

run.cmd: sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md/labmd | grep -E 'Raid Level|Array Size|State :|Active Devices|Working Devices|Failed Devices' | sed 's/^ *//'
run.output:
Raid Level : raid1
Array Size : 101376 (99.00 MiB 103.81 MB)
State : clean 
Active Devices : 2
Working Devices : 2
Failed Devices : 0

steps.title: Use it
steps.text: It is a normal block device. We put a file system on it and write a file.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/md/labmd; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/raid && sudo mount /dev/md/labmd /tmp/lab/raid && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/raid; echo 'survives a disk failure' > /tmp/lab/raid/data.txt; sync; cat /tmp/lab/raid/data.txt

steps.title: Fail one disk
steps.text: `--fail` marks a member as faulty (as the kernel does when it sees I/O errors). The array becomes **degraded** but keeps working. The `_` in `[U_]` marks the missing member.

run.cmd: cat /tmp/lab/raid/data.txt; echo 'written while degraded' >> /tmp/lab/raid/data.txt; sync; wc -l < /tmp/lab/raid/data.txt

steps.title: Replace and rebuild
steps.text: Remove the failed member, add a (new) one, and the array **resyncs** in the background. With a real replacement disk you would `--add` the new device.

run.cmd: sudo mdadm /dev/md/labmd --remove $L1 2>&1 | sed 's#/dev/loop[0-9]*#DISK#'; sudo mdadm /dev/md/labmd --add $L1 2>&1 | sed 's#/dev/loop[0-9]*#DISK#'; sleep 2
run.output:
mdadm: hot removed DISK from /dev/md/labmd
mdadm: added DISK

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Unmount, stop the array, wipe the RAID metadata, detach the loops.

run.cmd: sudo umount /tmp/lab/raid; sudo mdadm --stop /dev/md/labmd 2>&1 | sed -E 's#/dev/md[0-9]+#/dev/mdN#'; sudo mdadm --zero-superblock $L1 $L2; sudo losetup -d $L1 $L2; echo cleaned

steps.under: Each member has an **md superblock** (metadata 1.2 near the start of the device) with the array UUID, level, and an event counter. At assembly the kernel compares event counters to find which member is stale. RAID is **availability**, not backup: it faithfully mirrors a deleted file or a ransomware-encrypted one.

quiz.q: How many disk failures does RAID 1 with two disks survive?

options: No, it mirrors mistakes and deletions too
quiz.explain: RAID protects against hardware failure only.

quiz.q: Which tool manages Linux software RAID?

check.scenario: The monitoring shows `md0` degraded, `[U_]`. Walk through the replacement.
check.answer: `mdadm --detail /dev/md0` and `cat /proc/mdstat` to see which member failed; `smartctl` to confirm; `mdadm /dev/md0 --fail /dev/sdb1 --remove /dev/sdb1` if not already removed; replace the disk, copy the partition table (`sfdisk -d /dev/sda | sfdisk /dev/sdb`), `mdadm /dev/md0 --add /dev/sdb1`, watch the resync in `/proc/mdstat`, and reinstall the boot loader on the new disk if it is a boot array.

lessons.title: I/O schedulers and iostat
lessons.goal:
Learn how the kernel orders disk requests (the I/O scheduler), how to see the current one, and how to read `iostat` to judge whether a disk is busy.

Why it matters: "the disk is slow" is easy to say and hard to prove. `iostat -x` shows utilisation, latency and queue depth, so you can prove it.

setup.note: These steps use sudo and loop devices (image files acting as disks). They create a volume group called `labvg` and remove it at the end. They never touch real disks.

steps.title: The schedulers
steps.text: The **I/O scheduler** sits between the file system and the disk driver. Modern multi-queue (`blk-mq`) kernels offer: `none` (no reordering: best for fast NVMe SSDs), `mq-deadline` (guarantees each request a deadline, good default), `kyber` (latency targets for fast devices) and `bfq` (fair sharing between processes, good for desktops and slow disks).

steps.title: Change it (until reboot)
steps.text: Write a name into the file as root. Persist it with a udev rule or a tuned profile. We test on a loop device.

run.cmd: truncate -s 300M s.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show s.img); b=$(basename $L); cat /sys/block/$b/queue/scheduler

steps.title: Generate I/O and watch with iostat
steps.text: `iostat -x 1 2` prints extended statistics per device. The first report is the average since boot; the second covers the last second. We write to the loop device in the background while iostat samples it.

run.cmd: sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=$L bs=1M count=250 oflag=direct status=none & sleep 0.5; iostat -dx 1 2 $b | awk '$1=="'$b'" {w=$8; k=$9; a=$12; u=$NF} END {print "device w/s wkB/s w_await %util"; print "'$b'", w, k, a, u}'; wait

steps.after: Columns to read first: `w/s` (writes per second), `wkB/s` (throughput), `w_await` (average write latency in ms) and `%util` (how busy the device was). Because loop devices sit on a file, the numbers are only illustrative.

steps.title: How to read it
steps.text:
- **%util** near 100% on a single disk means saturated (not meaningful for SSDs/arrays that serve many requests in parallel).
- **await** (ms per request, queue + service) rising under load means queuing.
- **aqu-sz** (average queue size) above the number of parallel units means a backlog.
- High `%util` with low throughput suggests random small I/O.
steps.under: Throughput and latency are different questions. A disk can show 100% util at 5 MB/s (random 4 KB reads) and low util at 500 MB/s (sequential). Look at `await` and `aqu-sz` together with the workload type. `iotop`/`pidstat -d` attribute the I/O to processes.

quiz.q: Which scheduler is usually best for fast NVMe SSDs?
quiz.explain: `none` avoids needless work on fast devices.

quiz.q: Which iostat column is the average time a request waits and is served?
A single HDD shows %util 100 and await 80 ms. Is it saturated?
quiz.explain: High utilisation with high latency means it cannot keep up.

quiz.q: How do you persist an I/O scheduler choice?
quiz.explain: sysfs writes are lost at reboot.

check.scenario: An application complains of slow disk I/O. `iostat -x 1` shows `%util` 35% and `await` 2 ms on the data disk. What is your conclusion and next step?
check.answer: The disk is **not** the bottleneck: it is lightly used and fast. Look elsewhere: CPU (`mpstat`), memory pressure (`vmstat`), network or storage latency from the application's point of view (strace/`pidstat -d`), locks, or an NFS/remote volume instead of this disk.

interview.q: RAID 1, 5, 6 and 10: capacities and failures survived?
interview.a: RAID 1: 50% capacity, 1 failure. RAID 5: N-1 disks, 1 failure. RAID 6: N-2, 2 failures. RAID 10: 50%, one per mirror pair (at least 1). See [the lesson](#/lesson/22/mdadm-raid).
No. It protects against disk failure only. Deletion, corruption and ransomware are mirrored. You still need versioned backups.

interview.q: How do you decide whether a disk is the bottleneck?
interview.a: `iostat -x`: high %util with rising await and a growing queue (aqu-sz) mean saturation; low util means the problem is elsewhere. See [the lesson](#/lesson/22/io-schedulers-iostat).

A RAID array with a failed or missing member that still serves data.
The kernel component that orders block I/O requests.
